articles.title: RGB is the next big thing in OLED gaming monitors
articles.summary: LG Display and Samsung Display have announced panels that line up their subpixels in vertical RGB stripes for better clarity.
articles.body: New OLED gaming monitors from top companies coming out this year should look clearer and crisper. LG Display and Samsung Display, which typically provide the actual panels used in gaming monitors, are finally lining up the colors of their subpixels in vertical RGB stripes — remember when we used to worry about Pentile OLED displays? — which means, among other improvements, the panels should have easier-to-read text. You can see for yourself how Asus and MSI are touting changes to their upcoming monitors with Stripe RGB technology — for Asus, with the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM, ROG Swift OLED PG34WCDN, and ROG Strix OLED XG34WCDMS, and for MSI, with the MEG X and MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36: [Image: [Image: Both LG Display and Samsung Display aim to improve text clarity issues that have plagued ultrawide OLED panels in particular. Samsung Display announced earlier this month that it has started mass production of “the world’s first 34-inch 360Hz QD-OLED panel” with what it calls a “V-Stripe” RGB pixel structure. The V is a bit of a misnomer of how the structure is shaped; it indicates that the subpixels are in a vertical orientation, not in a V. The structure “improves the clarity of text edges, making it ideal for users engaged in text-intensive tasks such as document editing, coding, or content creation,” Samsung Display says. Samsung Display has already been “supplying the panels to seven global monitor manufacturers including ASUS, MSI, and Gigabyte since December 2025.” As for LG Display, it announced last month it would be debuting “the world’s first 27-inch 4K OLED panel for monitors featuring an RGB stripe structure and a 240Hz refresh rate” at CES in Las Vegas. While LG Display was previously known for “WOLED,” where its TVs and gaming monitors typically have an extra white subpixel, or orienting RGB pixels in a triangular pattern, the company says the RGB stripe panels are “optimized for operating systems such as Windows and for font-rendering engines, ensuring excellent text readability and high color accuracy” as well as for providing “optimal performance” in FPS games. Perhaps confusingly, “RGB stripe” isn’t the only new RGB screen tech from LG Display at CES. It’s also touting “Primary RGB Tandem 2.0,” which it calls “an advanced version of LG Display’s proprietary Primary RGB Tandem technology, which generates light by stacking the three primary colors of light (red, green, and blue) in independent layers.” As we discussed last year, Tandem OLED (and Primary RGB Tandem OLED specifically) are about dramatically increasing the brightness of OLED panels, which has been one of their few weaknesses over competing screen tech. Samsung Display’s QD-OLED panels use quantum dots to increase their panel brightness, whereas LG Display is now betting on these stacks. Asus says its PG27UCWM is both an RGB stripe panel and a Tandem OLED panel, though it’s not clear if it uses version 2.0. For gaming monitors, LG Display is promising that Primary RGB Tandem 2.0 will enable “monitor displays that achieve a peak brightness of up to 1,500 nits,” and up to 4,500 nits for OLED TVs using the tech. We were impressed by the 1.0 version of Primary RGB Tandem in the LG G5 TV, and we’ll be checking out 2.0 at CES.

articles.title: Shelly’s new $50 security camera watches your home without a subscription
articles.summary: The high-def camera can livestream to your phone or record events locally to a memory card.
articles.body: After launching a budget-friendly flood sensor last month with impressive battery life, Shelly announced a new $49.99 security camera today that can be used without any additional subscription fees — although that’s still an option if you want to expand its capabilities. The Shelly Camera will be available soon from the company’s online store and other resellers in black or white. Although competitors like Wyze have released 2K security cameras for $40, Shelly’s first camera is limited to 1080P with a wide field of view that stretches 110 degrees horizontally and 70 degrees vertically with night vision capabilities. But there’s no battery, so during installation you’ll also need to route a USB-C cable to deliver power. [Image: Wherever you decide to mount the Shelly Camera you’ll need to be mindful of cable management. When used without a subscription plan the camera can livestream video over Wi-Fi to various devices, capture events locally to a microSD card, and trigger smart home automations through other Shelly devices such as turning on a floodlight when movement is detected. If you do opt to pay for a subscription you’ll gain access to cloud recording as well as smart object detection that can distinguish between people, pets, and vehicles so alerts and automations can be customized for specific scenarios.

articles.title: GOP hard-liners threaten rebellion over stopgap funding bill
articles.summary: A small group of conservatives in the House of Representatives is threatening to vote against a procedural rule and stymie much of the GOP agenda for the week to protest a Senate-passed government funding bill the lower chamber is set to take up Tuesday. The hard-liners likely can’t block the funding bill itself, which is…
articles.body:
A small group of conservatives in the House of Representatives is threatening to vote against a procedural rule and stymie much of the GOP agenda for the week to protest a Senate-passed government funding bill the lower chamber is set to take up Tuesday.

The hard-liners likely can’t block the funding bill itself, which is known as a continuing resolution (CR) and would keep the government open through Dec. 11. The CR will come to the floor “under suspension,” meaning it doesn’t require a rule vote but will need a two-thirds majority to pass.

But the detractors could effectively freeze the floor and stall Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) from getting anything else done on the floor by tanking the rule, which would prevent other bills leadership wants passed from coming up for a vote.

Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) told reporters Monday night he’s voting no on the rule in an attempt to freeze the floor from other legislation.

He said he takes issue with several provisions in the Senate-passed CR, including its short-term delay on a ban on certain hemp products. He wants a “clean” continuing resolution or a chance to add his own priorities, like reupping a ban on federal funds going to Planned Parenthood that lapsed in the summer.

“All of this could’ve been handled either by putting it in the rule and allowing some amendments or just doing a clean CR, they didn’t do that,” Roy said of the Senate. “So I’ve got major problems with that.”

Roy sent a letter Monday to Reps. Tom Cole (R-Okla.) and Jodey Arrington (R-Texas), who chair the relevant committees on the CR, laying out his concerns.

Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.), chair of the House Freedom Caucus, also indicated he was against the rule as of Tuesday morning, citing concerns about the hemp ban delay. Rep. Pete Sessions (R-Texas), who is not usually one to defy leadership, also said Tuesday he would vote no.

Other Republicans have also voiced concerns about a provision in the Senate-passed CR that would delay a rule giving White House political appointees greater authority over whether to disburse federal grants.

Johnson can afford to lose just three Republicans on the rule vote, assuming every member is present and voting. But campaign season is in full swing, and dozens of lawmakers missed Monday night’s vote, which means attendance issues could create another complication.

Cole told reporters Tuesday morning he had not yet received Roy’s letter and said while he is “sympathetic” with Harris’s concerns about the hemp ban, it’s not worth risking a government shutdown before the midterm elections by changing or failing to pass the CR.

“This should not have been on here, CR should not be controversial, so I’m sympathetic with that,” Cole said.

He criticized the use of the rule as leverage, since traditionally, members are expected to vote with their party on the rule, regardless of how they plan to vote on the legislation itself.

“A lot of this is we’ve got a group that wants to leverage the procedural votes to extract things that the majority of us probably don’t want to do. I find that disappointing,” Cole said. “I mean, if you’re going to be a member of the Republican conference, you ought to be able to vote for the rule. It’s just that simple, and you shouldn’t use it to leverage things against your own team. You want to vote against the bill? That’s perfectly fine, and that’s true in any bill. Your final vote on the bill is up to you, but blackmailing your colleagues is not the way to build an effective team.”

Cole said he still expected solid support for the CR because he also anticipated that some Democrats would vote for it.

Others in the Freedom Caucus indicated they would support the rule. Rep. Ben Cline (R-Va.) told The Hill on Tuesday he generally supports rules and would vote for this one. Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) said he was “leaning toward voting for it” but would talk more with his colleagues first.

articles.title: MasterChef Winner Pankaj Bhadouria shares ‘Cancer’ changed her; says 'I was weakened by infections  that took a massive toll on my physical health'
articles.summary: MasterChef India Season 1 winner Pankaj Bhadouria, who was recently diagnosed with breast cancer, opened up about her ongoing treatment and shared an .
articles.body: MasterChef India Season 1 winner Pankaj Bhadouria, who was recently diagnosed with breast cancer, opened up about her ongoing treatment and shared an emotional update about the challenges she faced during August.Pankaj spoke about her battle with cancer and her second chemotherapy session. She also revealed repeated infections, hair loss and how August took a toll on her physical health. She also mentioned the moments of happiness she experienced with her family and friends.Pankaj took to her social media account and shared a photo from a hospital bed. She wrote, “August turned out to be quite eventful! It started with my second Chemotherapy that hit me really hard. It took a major toll on my health and hair too. Despite all precautions, preventive medicines and care, I was weakened by infections one after the other that took a massive toll on my physical health. And then came the other after effects- the major being hair loss! Believe me, nothing prepares you for it when it actually hits you. Losing my tresses was a shocker that took time coming to terms. But then, as the month moved on came in days that brought in joy and happiness- so many friends from far and near coming to visit me, celebrating festivals. I even snuck in a few sweets!”She added, “And then finally, an evening out with the family after 3 whole months! Yes, we ate out and it felt so good! It felt like a step towards recovery. It’s funny how a word like ‘Cancer’ changes your entire life and that of your family around you too. But then we are learning to live with it in the best way anyone can- with love, support and hope!”Pankaj has been sharing updates about her cancer journey with her followers on social media. Talking about Pankaj Bhadouria's cancer diagnosis, she first publicly revealed her breast cancer diagnosis on May 28, 2026. Sharing a picture from a hospital bed, she wrote, “I have been diagnosed with Breast Cancer. Need your prayers and support.”A day later, she shared that she was going in for surgery and thanked her fans for their love and support. She further revealed that her post-surgery biopsy detected a 2mm invasive HER2-positive component, after which doctors advised chemotherapy and targeted treatment.Before beginning chemotherapy, she had even chosen to cut her long hair short, saying she wanted to enjoy it while she had it.

articles.title: GoPro has been acquired and is getting into ‘defense, government, robotics and aerospace’
articles.summary: GoPro is now aimed at national security and defense, with a new buyer Starman Holdings and a YouTuber investor.
articles.body: GoPro suddenly looks like a very different company than it did just last week. First, YouTuber Mark “Markiplier” Fischbach became the company’s single largest shareholder, without disclosing that in a sponsored review that came out a week later. Now, almost the entire company has been bought by Starman Holding for $285 million in cash, which Starman is characterizing as a “merger.” While GoPro has always been best known as the company that makes consumer action cameras, the press release takes a bit of a different tone: founder and CEO Nick Woodman now calls GoPro “a leading American imaging and optical solutions company, addressing important areas of national security related to cameras, optics and AI infrastructure.” “The combination of GoPro’s world-class optical expertise and intellectual property with Starman’s advanced transceiver capabilities and U.S. manufacturing platform creates a unique opportunity. Together, we intend to bring production of these critical components back to the United States,” reads a quote from Starman Holdings CEO Charles Tebele. What is Starman Holding? According to Tebele’s online bio, it’s got a lot of fingers in a lot of pies — but you might recognize its phone case brands Incipio, Incase, Griffin, and Survivor. It appears that Starman Holding owns Onward Brands, which acquired Vinci Brands, a division of Armor Acquisition, which bought them from Incipio back in 2021. You might also recognize its brand Digital Gadgets, which reportedly donated to NY governor Kathy Hochul’s campaign around the same time it secured $637 million in contracts for COVID-19 tests, then sued the administration over subsequent bids. Amid its financial troubles — it had lost most of its value and had $92 million in debt — GoPro had already announced it would begin defense and aerospace consulting in April. The new press release says GoPro will “continue to fully support its existing consumer products” and grow in consumer, but it sounds a bit like a pivot. I’m just spitballing here, but when I think about tiny cameras, optical transceivers, and defense manufacturing, it reminds me of those long reels of optical fiber that come out the back of attack drones — and how US consumer drones have largely been set aside in favor of war. Starman says shareholders will keep 10 percent of the company’s shares; Markiplier purchased 8.5 percent. It’s not clear if the YouTuber plans to keep them, or will get a rapid payday; the value of the stock doubled overnight, though it’s currently settling down. [Image: The deal should close by the end of the year, according to the press release; it does not yet appear to have hit the SEC’s filing system yet.

articles.title: Homey just made the smart home controller I hoped Apple would build
articles.summary: The LG-owned smart home platform is launching a $299 controller that works with thousands of devices — but you’ll want a Homey hub
articles.body: Smart homes have gotten really good at making things really complicated. Turning on a light can involve multiple steps, compared to just flipping a switch. Homey, the Dutch-based smart home platform owned by LG, thinks it has a solution. This week it launched the Homey Portal, a touchscreen smart home controller that looks very promising, if very expensive. Preorders open today at an introductory price of $249/€249, with units shipping in December. A 2.8-inch round touchscreen device with a stainless steel dial, the Homey Portal can sit on a desk or mount to the wall and is powered by a USB-C cable. You tap the icons to control devices like lights, speakers, thermostats, and shades, and you can twist the dial to adjust brightness, volume, and temperature. [Video: Homey Portal smart home controller] The idea of a dedicated smart home control device that can connect to everything in a smart home is compelling. App, voice, and button control have their place, but they’re not as easy as walking up to a switch and just knowing what to do. The problem so far has been interoperability; not everything works with everything. Homey, with its claimed support for over 70,000 devices from over 2,000 brands, plus Matter, Zigbee, Z-Wave, and Thread, is well-positioned to tackle this. The Portal invites comparisons to an Echo Show or Google Nest Hub, but it feels more focused. “We’ve always wanted a smart home to feel as simple as flipping a light switch,” said Stefan Witkamp, CEO at Athom, Homey’s parent company. It’s designed to give a direct, physical way to control your home, “instead of doing everything through an app,” he said. In many ways, the Portal looks like the smart home controller I’ve always envisioned Apple building for Apple Home: simple, intuitive, and uncluttered. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: In Homey’s demo video, the interface adapts its UI to each action you want to take. For example, tapping the lights icon brings up a screen to turn the room’s lights on or off and adjust the color; then you can adjust the brightness by twisting the dial. There’s also a weather icon that shows a short forecast along with a built-in timer. The screen is customizable, letting you add controls for different elements of your smart home, and it works with Homey’s Flow automation engine, so you can trigger scenes and automations. Homey demoed setting up a livestream of your doorbell camera to appear on the Portal when it rings, along with a prompt to open your smart lock. There’s no microphone, so no voice control;Homey integrates with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Siri Shortcuts for voice control. The company says the Portal is designed to be set up for different zones in a home, such as the kitchen, living room, and bedroom. Along with controls for that room, it can monitor and manage energy use in each. But at $299/€299 after the introductory price, outfitting three rooms would cost nearly $900 — and that’s before adding a Homey hub. [Image: The Portal works with Homey Pro, Homey Pro mini, Homey Cloud (free for up to 5 devices), and Homey Self-Hosted Server. The Portal itself isn’t a hub and requires a connection to one of Homey’s platform options: the Homey Cloud for $3.99 a month (free for up to 5 devices), the Homey Pro Mini hub ($249), a 2023 or later Homey Pro hub ($449), or a self-hosted Homey server on your own hardware. The benefit of the hubs is local communication. Compatible devices will continue to run without an internet connection and can still be controlled by the Portal, according to Homey. The company also just announced a new device update feature that allows you to update Matter, Z-Wave, and Zigbee devices directly through Homey; no need to use the manufacturer’s hub or app. Homey, which was founded in 2014, draws comparisons to Home Assistant, with its selling point being a more plug-and-play setup. However, Homey is closed-source and now owned by LG, whereas Home Assistant remains an open-source platform managed by the nonprofit Open Home Foundation. Homey runs as an independent smart home platform today, but also integrates with LG’s AI Home platform, with a focus on home energy management. We’ve seen several companies launch smart switches with displays that similarly try to solve the control problem, including Aqara, Shelly, and Brilliant, but most require hardwiring and don’t have as many integrations as Homey. Homey’s advantage appears to be ease of installation and breadth of support. I’ll be checking out the Portal in person this week at the IFA tech show in Berlin and look forward to testing it to see if it can earn a spot in my smart home.

articles.title: Apple Officially Has a New CEO, but What Does That Mean?
articles.body:
Apple announced back in April that Tim Cook was stepping down as CEO, and that John Ternus would replace him on September 1. That day has finally arrived, and Tim Cook is no longer in charge of the company – though he remains leading the board of directors.

Tim Cook took the reigns from Steve Jobs all the way back in 2011 and has grown Apple to be one of the biggest companies in the world. During his tenure, Apple debuted the Apple Watch, the Vision Pro, and the company even started making its own CPUs. But it's important to keep in mind that Cook got his start at the company in operations, which is probably a huge reason why Apple grew to focus so much on manufacturing its own hardware.

Ternus, on the other hand, started out as an engineer and has spent time in charge of designing everything from iPhones to Apple Watch, the latter of which has been particularly successful. It's obviously too early to tell what impact Ternus is going to have on the company as a whole, but that doesn't mean I can't speculate a bit about it.

Analysts have already gone on record and said that Ternus' main goal will likely be leading Apple into the age of AI. Whether you love AI or hate it, Apple has fallen short in its implementation of the technology, often leaning on solutions from other companies, like ChatGPT, to power a lot of its Apple Intelligence software suite.

Because Ternus' background has been leading hardware engineering throughout the company, he will likely be trying to solve Apple's AI problems through hardware. Apple's iPhone event is next week , and it's going to be the first Apple keynote with Ternus emceeing. If nothing else, that helps lead credence to the rumors that Apple will finally be revealing its first foldable this year. And if that foldable does exist, it's likely that the new CEO has had a big hand in designing the thing.

Even looking further out, I'd like to imagine that Ternus' time as CEO will lead to more hardware innovation. Apple has had a few hits in the Tim Cook years, but it's also had some flops, like the Apple Vision Pro . To this day, I still don't know quite what Apple was thinking by releasing a $3,499 (now $3,699) AR headset in 2024.

Regardless, I'd love to see Apple create something truly groundbreaking again. I'm not sure if John Ternus is going to be the next Steve Jobs, but he probably has a better chance of doing that than Tim Cook ever did. It's time to let the engineer cook.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: Google Find Hub will soon help you locate things without a tracker
articles.summary: New features coming to Android this month include locating important items without a tracker, a solution for motion sickness, and themes for Google Messages.
articles.body: Google announced new features coming to Android devices as part of this month’s feature drop update. Among the highlights are the introduction of Motion Assist — Android’s version of Apple’s Motion Cues feature, which tries to reduce motion sickness by overlaying dots on your screen that move in response to a vehicle’s movements — as well as an expansion of Find Hub. The Find Hub update will introduce a new way to find important items without having to attach a tracker. According to a Google blog post shared today, you’ll soon be able to ask Gemini to remember where you put an important item like a passport that you don’t frequently use and may forget exactly where you stashed months later. Gemini will save its location and let you add a photo. When you need it again, you can ask Gemini for that location, or find the item in Find Hub’s remembered items tab. The feature will be available on devices running Android 16 or later in countries where both Gemini and Find Hub are supported. [Media: Other updates include Guided Vision, which uses your phone’s camera in Gemini Live to help you read the fine print on labels or menus or locate items such as a specific ingredient in the cupboard. The feature provides voice feedback if the camera framing isn’t lined up properly, and is coming to devices running at least Android 9. Chat themes for Google Messages are also now available, letting you select a background image that text bubbles will automatically match. And starting today, everyone in a Google Messages chat can create and edit notes through Google Keep, so you can collaborate on a shared grocery list or trip planning.

articles.title: Who is John Ternus, the new Apple CEO? | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Starting on September 1, Ternus will lead one of the world's most valuable companies, but if you're not a dedicated Apple enthusiast, you've probably never heard of this man, who has largely remained out of the spotlight until now.
articles.body:
After 15 years, Tim Cook has handed off the Apple CEO role to John Ternus, the company’s senior vice president of hardware engineering. As of Tuesday, Ternus now leads one of the world’s most valuable companies. But if you’re not a dedicated Apple enthusiast, you’ve probably never heard of this man, who has largely remained out of the spotlight until he was announced as Cook’s successor in April.

Ternus is assuming the CEO role at a crucial time for Apple. Next week, the company will host its iPhone launch event , ushering in its newest line of hardware. Apple will also soon roll out its new-and-improved Siri AI experience, which is powered by Google’s Gemini.

“I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John,” Tim Cook wrote to staff on his last day as CEO. “Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does and I could not be more excited for his leadership.”

Cook will remain at Apple as executive chairman.

How long has John Ternus worked at Apple?

Ternus has worked at Apple for nearly half of his life — now 51 years old, he has been with the company for 25 years.

He joined Apple’s product design team in 2001 as only his second job out of college (his first was at a small maker of virtual-reality devices called Virtual Research Systems). By 2013, Ternus was a VP of hardware engineering and was promoted to the SVP role in 2021.

Ternus — who is 15 years younger than Cook — was among the youngest of top Apple executives who had been rumored as a possible successor, implying that Apple could be looking for someone to lead the company for a long time. After all, Apple has only had two CEOs in this millennium, so it seems that leadership continuity is important to the company.

Ternus previously reported to Cook, who he considers a mentor, and led all of hardware engineering at Apple. That’s a pretty big deal for a company that’s known for ubiquitous hardware like the iPhone and the MacBook.

In his 2024 commencement speech at his alma mater, the University of Pennsylvania’s engineering school, Ternus reflected on the lessons he learned at Apple, which perhaps can tell us a bit about his character — or at least a sanitized version of it.

“Always assume you’re as smart as anyone else in the room, but never assume that you know as much as they do,” Ternus said in the speech. “With this mindset, you’ll find the confidence you need to push forward, but more importantly, the humility to ask questions.”

In a tech ecosystem populated with abrasive egos, it’s refreshing to hear Ternus utter the word “humility.” Better yet, he only just joined X!

Ternus’ earliest project at Apple involved scrutinizing parts for the Apple Cinema Display, an early desktop monitor.

“At some point in my first year, I found myself at a supplier facility. I was far away from home. Well past midnight, I was using a magnifying glass to count the number of grooves on the head of a screw … and I was arguing with the supplier because these parts had 35 grooves. They were supposed to have 25,” Ternus recalled in his commencement speech. “I distinctly remember stepping back for a minute and thinking, ‘What the hell am I doing? Is this normal?’”

As Ternus climbed the corporate ladder, his responsibilities grew. He may no longer spend as much time analyzing screws, but he still seems to take pride in getting the little details right. In a recent interview , when Ternus was asked about his favorite memory of Steve Jobs, he mentioned the former Apple co-founder’s attention to craftsmanship.

“[Jobs] was moving a piece of furniture, a chest of drawers, and pulled it away from the wall and looked at the back and was just reflecting on, you know, that the carpenter who made it had made it beautiful,” Ternus said. “It finished the back as beautifully as the rest of it, even though nobody was going to see it, right? And I think about that all the time because I think that perfectly exemplifies what we do here.”

From there, he went on to lead the hardware development behind products across the Apple ecosystem, overseeing launches like AirPods, Apple Watch, and the Vision Pro. He also had a hand in major technical upgrades at Apple, like Apple’s transition from Intel chips to its own proprietary Apple silicon .

Most recently, Ternus was involved in the production of the MacBook Neo , Apple’s new, more affordable laptop model that lowers costs through some clever trade-offs in hardware design, like using an iPhone chip to power the device.

“We never want to ship junk. We want to ship great products that have that Apple experience, that Apple quality. To do that with the Neo required building something completely new from the ground up … leveraging both the technologies we’d been developing like Apple silicon, but also the kind of expertise that we’ve developed over many, many years of building Macs, and building phones, and building iPads, and all of these things,” Ternus told Tom’s Guide .

As CEO, Ternus will have to steer Apple through its challenge to catch up in the AI race and figure out what to do with the underlying tech behind the Vision Pro.

Ternus was on the swim team at Penn. For his senior project, he built a feeding arm that people with quadriplegia could control with head movements.

According to public records of political donations, Ternus donated $2,900 to Senator Chuck Schumer (D-NY) in 2021.

Otherwise, Ternus has maintained a relatively low profile.

articles.title: John Ternus sends first memo as Apple CEO teasing a ‘huge launch next week’
articles.summary: John Ternus’s first staff memo as Apple’s new CEO is pointing directly at its iPhone launch event next week.
articles.body: New Apple CEO John Ternus sent out his first staff memo, thanking his predecessor Tim Cook, and quickly turning to what the company will do next, reports Bloomberg. “We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible,” writes Ternus, referring to the September 9th event where Apple’s expected to unveil new iPhones including the rumored foldable iPhone Ultra and iPhone 18 Pro models. Ternus also hints at “incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet,” presumably moving beyond camera-equipped AirPods, home robots, and even more OLED displays. > Team, > Today, on my first day as CEO, I just wanted to send a quick note to thank everyone for the warm wishes. I also want to extend my deep appreciation to Tim for sharing so much of his knowledge and experience during this transition, and more importantly, for everything he contributed to Apple over the years. We’re so lucky to have had a CEO who led with his values and with such decency and humanity. We are all better for it and I’m so grateful he’ll be our executive chairman. > I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store. We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible. > I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet that we’ll dream up and create together. There’s no team in the world I’d rather build the future with. > More to come. In the meantime, thanks for your excellent work! > John

articles.title: John Ternus hypes 'huge launch next week' in first memo as Apple CEO | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Apple is hosting its iPhone release event next week, which is rumored to feature the first-ever foldable iPhone.
articles.body:
John Ternus has officially taken the reins as Apple CEO, succeeding Tim Cook, who held the role for 15 years.

The company’s former senior vice president of Hardware Engineering, Ternus enters the CEO role at a critical time for Apple. On September 9, the company will host its annual iPhone event, which is rumored to include the launch of Apple’s first foldable iPhone . Apple is also expected to roll out its new-and-improved Siri AI more broadly, which marks an important opportunity for the company to position Siri as an equal to chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude.

“We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal,” Ternus wrote in a memo to staff on Tuesday, according to Bloomberg. “I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet that we’ll dream up and create together.”

Apple is rumored to be working on several new products, like camera-equipped AirPods , smart glasses , and a touchscreen laptop .

“I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John,” Tim Cook wrote to staff on his last day as CEO. “Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does and I could not be more excited for his leadership.”

articles.title: This CD player that’s smaller than a CD has me asking questions.
articles.summary:
While the Sony D-88 is the first player smaller than a CD, the $100 Fosi Disc Nano I saw at CanJam SoCal is super cool, even if playing a disc while carrying it seems dangerous. It has both 3.5mm and 4.4mm outputs, Bluetooth connectivity, and comes out later this month.

articles.title: Google's Android update tackles motion sickness, accessibility, and more | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The new features coming to Android are aimed at reducing motion sickness, helping blind users navigate their surroundings, and more.
articles.body:
On Tuesday, Google announced it’s rolling out five new updates designed to make Android phones more accessible, useful, and personalized. Announced in a blog post on Tuesday, the features include those aimed at reducing motion sickness, helping blind and low-vision users navigate their surroundings, remembering where users leave important items, and another that adds new ways to personalize Google Messages.

While some of the features see Google playing catch-up to Apple, which already offers similar features for iPhone users, others specifically leverage Gemini to provide various improvements.

The most interesting update is “Motion Assist,” a feature designed to help people who experience motion sickness while using their phones in a moving vehicle. It adds a bubble overlay to the screen that moves in response to the vehicle’s motion, helping reduce the disconnect between what users see on their screens and what their bodies feel.

The concept isn’t entirely new, however. Apple introduced “ Vehicle Motion Cues ” in 2024, which uses animated dots around the edges of the display that move in response to a vehicle’s motion.

Users can set “Motion Assist” to turn on automatically, add it to Quick Settings, and customize the bubble’s shape, color, and transparency. Google says this feature is available to Android 17 users.

Google is also introducing “Guided Vision,” a feature designed with blind and low-vision users in mind. It combines the phone’s camera with Gemini to help with tasks such as reading small print on a food label, viewing a menu in a dark restaurant, or identifying objects around the house.

The feature can also provide voice guidance when the camera isn’t positioned correctly, telling users to move the phone, pan around, or center an object. Guided Vision is coming to phones running Android 9 and newer in countries where Gemini is available.

Another update gives Gemini a new way to help users remember where they put important items. A “remembered items” section in Find Hub will allow users to tell Gemini where they’ve stored something. For example, a user could say they put their passport in a bedroom drawer, and Gemini can save that information in Find Hub. Users can also attach a photo to make the item easier to identify later.

Additionally, Google is adding a Google Keep integration to Google Messages, allowing people to share and edit grocery lists, vacation notes, and other information directly within a conversation.

Plus, Google Messages is getting more personalization options. Users will be able to customize individual chats with backgrounds, photos, and colors, Google says. The text bubbles will automatically match.

Apple added a similar custom background feature to Messages last year.

articles.title: Lenovo’s 2-in-1 Yoga 7i is a great Labor Day deal at $750
articles.summary: This discounted Lenovo 2-in-1 has an Intel Core 7 Ultra CPU, 16GB of LPDDRX5 memory, and a 512GB SSD, all packed into a slim laptop with a 360-degree hinge.
articles.body: Best Buy is celebrating Labor Day all week long with big deals, including a deep discount on the Lenovo Yoga 7i 2-in-1, taking its original $1,1199.99 price down to $749.99. It’s a capable configuration for the price, with a Core 7 Ultra 256V processor, 16GB of LPDDR5X memory, and a 512GB SSD. The IPS touchscreen has a 1920 x 1200 resolution with a 60Hz refresh rate, good enough for scrolling, taking notes, or catching up on YouTube videos. It can be tough to find a laptop at this price that doesn’t cut corners, and this model fits well within our criteria for a laptop suited for school and casual use. [Product: Lenovo Yoga 7i 2-in-1 | Notably, this model is a 2-in-1 and features a 360-degree hinge, letting you fold the device all the way around to use it like a tablet, or prop it up on a surface for watching content. With an advertised battery life of up to 12.5 hours per charge, you shouldn’t have any issues getting through a full day of classes and studying, or just mucking about on Reddit.

articles.title: This new Roomba seals itself to your carpet
articles.summary: The Roomba Max 875 and Plus 678 use a new SealForce to pull more dirt out of carpet.
articles.body: iRobot has announced a new flagship robot vacuum, which it will showcase at IFA in Berlin this week, the company’s first big tech trade show in years. The Roomba maker will be exhibiting under its new owner, Picea Robotics, the contract manufacturer that purchased the once-troubled American robotics company out of bankruptcy in January. The $1,199 Roomba Max 875 Combo is the company’s newest top-of-the-line robot vacuum and mop, and it debuts alongside the $899 Roomba Plus 678 Combo. Both models are available now at irobot.com. The key vacuuming improvement is a new sealing system iRobot is calling SealForce that takes vacuuming “to a level beyond what’s previously been possible,” iRobot chief engineer Adam Pope said. This works by lowering a sort of skirt around the cleaning head when it detects carpet, enabling a better seal that directs airflow deeper into the carpet. Paired with a new vane-type blower motor that Pope says moves 20 L/s (liters of air per second), SealForce helps the Roomba 875 deliver three times deeper carpet cleaning than without the feature. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The 875 offers 35,000 Pa suction power, the highest iRobot has ever published—for years, the company refused to publish detailed suction-power specs. It uses a single rubber brush rather than the company’s signature dual rollers (my favorite for pet hair on carpet). Pope says this is to accommodate that better seal against the carpet. It uses lidar and camera-based vision to navigate and detect obstacles and has a slimmer footprint than the Roomba 775. It can also climb thresholds up to 3.5 cm high. [Image: The 875 has a roller mop that can extend to the side to clean edges and a new hair-cutting anti-tangle brush. The 875 Combo is also a mopping robot, with a self-cleaning roller mopping system that adds more downward pressure than the 775, plus a new heated mist feature called ThermaMist, which sprays ahead of the mop to pretreat stains. The mop includes a retractable mop cover that extends during vacuuming to keep carpets dry and can extend to get along edges. The robot comes with an auto-empty / wash dock that automatically washes the mop with hot water and dries it with hot air. This SealForce tech is new to iRobot, but not to robot vacuums; Narwal and Dreame have variations on this on their latest flagships, the Narwal Flow 2 and Dreame X60 Max Ultra. But it is novel in the space, and combined with ThermaMist, a new hair-cutting anti-tangle main brush, and an anti-tangle side brush, the 875 shows that iRobot is inching closer to catching up with its competition than with its last relaunch. [Image: [Image: The company is releasing a midrange version of the 875, the Roomba Plus 678 Combo. This also has a roller mop and the new SealForce tech, but it drops to 30,000Pa suction power and 18 L/s of airflow, and there’s no ThermaMist or mop cover. Instead, the 678 has its own treatment system called SprayForce, which sprays cleaning fluid on stains to presoak them, then comes back later. It lifts its mop 10mm when it detects carpet. Both new models work with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Siri Shortcuts, and are currently going through Matter certification, according to Pope. A robot vacuum with better vacuuming is less flashy but more practical than those that sprout legs and arms. We’re seeing several manufacturers adopt this type of sealing technology — one upright vacuum makers have been trying to perfect for decades. It will be interesting to see if Roomba’s version solves that very real problem when it comes to cleaning carpet.

articles.title: Dell’s newest laptop sounds a lot like a MacBook Neo
articles.summary: Dell’s new Dell 14S is a colorful laptop aimed at students, starting with 8GB of RAM and sporting Intel’s Wildcat Lake chips.
articles.body: Dell’s new Dell 14S laptop sounds a lot like a MacBook Neo: it comes in four colors, is aimed at students, and it starts with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. Announced at IFA 2026, the 14S is meant to sit below the recently launched XPS 13 and offer another affordable laptop option as most other models continue to climb in price. The 14S will come in linen (beige), dusty rose (pink), washed denim (blue), and velvet green (yep, that’s green). That’s much more colorful than the XPS 13, and like its fancier brethren, the 14S can be configured with 16GB of RAM and a 512GB or 1TB SSD. The Dell 14S isn’t as thin or as light as the XPS 13, but in addition to the same two USB-C 3.2 Gen 2 ports with DisplayPort and Power Delivery, it also has HDMI 1.4 and a 3.5mm audio jack. (Why the XPS 13 lacks a headphone jack, I’ll never understand). But the 14S has much more basic, non-touch display options: a 300-nit 1920 x 1200 / 60Hz LCD or a 450-nit 2880 x 1800 / 120Hz one. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: There are some other niceties for students on the 14S, including a 1080p webcam with Windows Hello face unlock support, and battery life that Dell claims can last for up to 23 hours of Netflix streaming. For chip offerings, it’ll be either the Intel Core 5 320 or Core 7 350 — the 14S won’t scale up to Intel Panther Lake options like the XPS 13 is soon expected to. We don’t know how much any of this will cost just yet, as pricing is TBD for now, but in a virtual briefing Dell reps said the 14S will be close to the XPS 13’s $700 starting price yet slightly more accessible. We’ll know actual prices closer to its release later this fall. I’m currently testing and reviewing the XPS 13, and I’ve been very impressed with the hardware (except for the missing headphone jack). I’m all for seeing more good, affordable laptops out there — hopefully the 14S makes the right compromises to get the price down.
